svg.aria-label: The eight stages at which gene expression can be controlled and the character of each, showing the resource-saving logic that makes transcription initiation the main control point and the speed advantage of the later stages as a cost versus speed trade-off.
svg.text: The eight stages, from DNA access to protein destruction
1 Chromatin state: is the DNA accessible?
2 TRANSCRIPTION INITIATION
3 Elongation and termination
4 RNA processing (alternative splicing)
5 Nuclear export and localization
6 mRNA stability (half-life)
7 Translation initiation
8 Modification and degradation
The trade-off along this axis
Early stages are ECONOMICAL
Switch off at the front and every downstream cost disappears with it.
No mRNA means no template, so no amino acids and no ATP are spent.
This is why transcription initiation is the most widely used control point.
Late stages are FAST
Starting from transcription takes tens of minutes. Switching on the
translation of stored mRNA, or activating stored protein, takes seconds.
An egg divides on stored mRNA after fertilization without transcribing anything.
How to read this
Before discussing control, name the stage. "Gene X is upregulated" does
not say whether more RNA is made, less is destroyed, or more is translated.
Which stage a gene uses tells you what that gene is required to do.
